content:
Touma woke to find Mio in the corner.

Not her voice. Not the familiar pressure of her presence, or a private comment arriving before he was awake enough to defend himself against it.

Mio herself, visible against the wall, studying the room as if it might have teeth hidden somewhere.

He stared.

“You can’t be there,” he said.

Her attention shifted to him. “Apparently I can.”

“I mean—there.”

“That doesn’t improve the argument.”

The ceiling was the same suspicious beige. The broken lamp was still broken. Dust, instant coffee, and cheap disinfectant still accounted for most of the air. Nothing about the safehouse had changed except that his private wrongness was now standing in the corner, like a clerical error large enough to become visible.

His face grew hot.

“Stop staring,” Mio said.

“I’m checking something.”

“With your eyes fixed on me.”

“I thought you might disappear if I blinked.”

“You’ve blinked.”

He had. Several times.

She remained.

Until now, there had been a layer between the strange thing happening to him and the rest of the world. It hadn’t been a particularly reassuring layer, but it had existed. He could hear something nobody else heard. He could answer under his breath. He could pretend, badly, that all of it belonged inside his head.

Now she occupied a place in the room.

He sat up and reached for the blanket slipping off the futon.

His hand went through her knee.

There was no resistance. His fingers closed on the blanket beyond her, and for a moment his mind refused to put the two facts together: he could see her leg, and his arm was passing through it.

He pulled back.

Mio recoiled a fraction later. The movement had a slight lag, as though the thought had needed to ask the room for permission before becoming motion.

“Warn me before you do that.”

“I didn’t mean to.”

“That’s what makes it worse.”

He drew the blanket into his lap, carefully this time.

She had come closer while he was looking away. Or he hadn’t understood how close she already was. Either possibility made him feel suddenly unqualified to move his own arms.

“Can you feel anything?”

Mio looked at him.

“Physically or emotionally?”

“I meant physically.”

“Then ask that.”

“Could you stop acting like a person who understands me too well for one minute?”

“That was always the case.”

It was worse with a face attached.

He looked down at the blanket. What he remembered of the procedure returned in pieces: instructions, the effort of following them, Nico saying something that had sounded reassuring only because Touma had desperately needed it to. None of those pieces explained what he was supposed to do with Mio standing beside his bed.

She moved back to give him space.

Again, that almost imperceptible delay.

He watched her shoulders tighten. Watched her take a breath before answering a question he hadn’t yet managed to ask. Her hands shifted, then stopped, as if she was still deciding where they belonged when someone could see them.

She seemed more alive than she had when she was only audible.

That wasn’t a thought he liked having. She had been there before. She had argued, noticed things, understood him with intolerable accuracy. Visibility shouldn’t have made any difference to what she was.

But now he could see that she was afraid.

He couldn’t safely file the fear under tone, or imagine he had misunderstood it. It was there in the careful set of her shoulders and the way she kept checking the room without turning her head too quickly.

Touma got up.

There was barely enough floor between the futon and the kitchenette counter to pace, but he tried. Three steps one way, turn, three steps back.

He kept glancing at her.

He knew where the counter was. He knew where the wall was. He should have been able to walk the narrow strip without recalculating the room every time he turned.

Instead, his body kept treating her as its center.

He gave her space she apparently didn’t physically need. He caught himself turning sideways to pass her. When she watched him, being watched was no longer something happening privately inside his skull. It had a direction.

This wasn’t even a tactical problem yet.

It was a social one.

Somehow that felt less manageable.

The door opened.

Touma stopped pacing.

Nico stood in the doorway, one hand still on the handle. His eyes went first to Touma, then to Mio. They stayed on her a little too long.

“You’re both awake.”

“You knew she could do that?” Touma asked.

“No.”

Too fast.

Nico seemed to hear it too. He adjusted his grip on the handle.

“No,” he repeated, more deliberately. “I knew there could be effects outside the expected range. I didn’t know this would be one of them.”

“This,” Mio said.

Nico’s mouth tightened.

Touma had the unpleasant impression that Nico was accustomed to problems that stayed inside closed systems. You checked the readings, changed something, checked again.

This problem could look back at him.

And object to his choice of words.

Then another piece of the procedure came back to Touma: the witness rule.

He looked from Nico to the threshold.

“That still applies?”

Nico followed his glance. “Yes.”

The open doorway suddenly seemed wider than it had a moment ago. Nico stepped inside and shut the door, carefully enough to make the care noticeable.

“The limiter is stable for the moment,” he said. “The projection isn’t.”

“Projection,” Touma repeated.

“I’m using the most accurate term I have.”

“It makes her sound like a school presentation.”

“I’m not defending the terminology.”

“You’re certainly relying on it,” Mio said.

Nico looked at her again. He was trying hard to keep his expression neutral. Touma could see the work involved.

“We need to distinguish the side effect from—”

“The side effect looks like a person,” Touma said.

“Yes. That’s why precision matters.”

Touma glanced at Mio, expecting at least some agreement.

“Nico isn’t wrong,” she said.

“You’re taking his side?”

“I’m taking the side where we continue existing.”

That ended the argument more effectively than Touma wanted it to.

Nico let out a small breath.

“Visibility may not be limited to what happens in this room.”

Touma looked at the closed door.

“Someone outside could see her?”

“Possibly. But I don’t just mean people.”

The room seemed to lose another degree of privacy.

“What do you mean?”

“Cameras. Biometric systems. Active recognition filters.” Nico paused between each item, as if checking how much certainty the words could bear. “Other systems may be able to register her now.”

“Register her as what?”

“I don’t know.”

Touma looked at Mio. She stood very still.

He thought of the clerk outside, of the ordinary effort of passing through public spaces without becoming memorable. A person could look away. A camera didn’t need to be interested. Somewhere beyond the room, a filter could notice a shape it couldn’t classify and keep it anyway.

“And humans?” he asked.

“Possibly,” Nico said. “We don’t know how broadly this extends.”

“So we don’t know who can see her, what can record her, or how long this lasts.”

“Correct.”

Mio’s outline was steady, but Touma remembered the delay in her movements. Bad signal. Passwords that wouldn’t stay the same. Nothing solid enough to trust, and suddenly far too much for the world to notice.

He had thought waking up to her beside the futon was the problem.

“How bad is that?” he asked.

Nico glanced at Mio, then back at him.

“Bad enough for you.”
